design_detail: Secondary analysis comparing two cohorts drawn from the pre-randomization phase of two residential research trials at one US research unit (Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit, Baltimore): 103 adults with opioid dependence enrolled 2010 to 2015, before fentanyl reached the local supply and with urine positive for non-fentanyl opioids (Non-Fentanyl study), and 30 adults with opioid use disorder enrolled 2021 to February 2024 with fentanyl-positive urine (Fentanyl study). Both received the same fixed morphine stabilization for a week on the same unit, with withdrawal rated four times a day. The authors call it quasi-experimental; exposure was not assigned and the comparison group is historical.
can_establish: Whether, under one identical fixed morphine stabilization regimen in one residential unit, people entering with fentanyl exposure reported and showed more withdrawal symptoms, with a different day-by-day course, than people who entered a decade earlier with non-fentanyl opioid exposure.
cannot_establish: That fentanyl itself causes more severe withdrawal (the groups differ in era, parent trial, eligibility, age and concomitant medicines, and other adulterants such as xylazine or nitazenes could not be ruled out); the course of untreated withdrawal after stopping fentanyl (everyone was receiving morphine, so the outcome is withdrawal despite a fixed morphine regimen); effects beyond one week; how often severe withdrawal occurs outside research settings; or effect sizes (none are reported).

sample.recruitment: Adults with opioid use disorder recruited from the community into two randomized residential trials of opioid tapering at the same unit: tramadol extended-release against clonidine and buprenorphine (NCT01188421; October 2010 to June 2015) and a percutaneous nerve-stimulator device against lofexidine with placebo or sham (NCT04325659; enrolment from March 2021, ongoing; participants up to February 2024 included) (Methods › Parent Trials).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Non-Fentanyl trial: ages 18 to 60, DSM-IV opioid dependence, urine evidence of recent opioid use, no significant medical or psychiatric illness. Fentanyl trial: ages 22 to 65, DSM-5 opioid use disorder, urine evidence of recent opioid use, no significant medical or psychiatric illness. Both excluded pregnancy, physical dependence on alcohol or benzodiazepines needing withdrawal treatment, allergy to study medicines and current opioid agonist treatment. Full criteria in a supplementary table (not read).
sample.demographics: Combined: 56% Black or African American, 40% non-Hispanic White, 4% other; 84% men (Fentanyl study 76.7%, Non-Fentanyl 85.4%); 79% with at least high-school education. The Fentanyl group was older: mean age 46.0 (SD 10.1) against 41.2 (SD 10.2), p = 0.021; no other demographic difference was significant (Results › Participants; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not reported: the paper does not say how many participants contributed ratings on each stabilization day or whether anyone left during the stabilization week.
sample.selection_effects: Both cohorts volunteered for residential research trials of withdrawal management, which selects people willing to stop opioids under study conditions. The Fentanyl cohort is the first 30 of an ongoing trial. Different eras (about a decade apart), different diagnostic manuals and age limits, and urine confirmation of non-fentanyl status by chromatography in only 3 of 103 participants.

exposure.measurement: Urine at entry: all Fentanyl-study participants tested positive for fentanyl; all Non-Fentanyl participants tested positive on an opioid immunoassay with a morphine standard (which does not detect fentanyl), and the 3 tested by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (all in the final study year) had no fentanyl or norfentanyl. Amount, frequency, route and duration of use and other drugs in the urine are not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study condition (the outcome period): immediate-release morphine 30 mg by subcutaneous injection four times a day for 7 days in both cohorts, on the same residential unit, before randomization in the parent trials. Withdrawal ratings and vital signs four times daily; analyses use each day's peak rating, days 1 to 7. In the Fentanyl trial only, protocolized concomitant medicines were available for withdrawal symptoms during stabilization (acetaminophen, antacid, clonazepam, dicyclomine, hydroxyzine, ibuprofen, loperamide, methocarbamol, milk of magnesia, ondansetron, promethazine, simethicone, trazodone), given after each data-collection time point.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported. Both trials excluded physical dependence on alcohol or benzodiazepines needing withdrawal treatment. The authors note that xylazine had entered the local fentanyl supply and that nitazenes or other synthetic opioids may have been present; neither was measured.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Participants were in early abstinence from illicit opioids, receiving fixed morphine; time since last use at admission is not reported.

comparison.controls: Historical cohort: participants of the earlier trial with non-fentanyl opioid exposure, stabilized with the same morphine regimen on the same unit.
comparison.matching: None; no adjustment for age (the one demographic difference) or for era. Analyses are unadjusted two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychiatric comorbidity, pain, body mass index (which the authors link to fentanyl clearance), amount and duration of opioid use and other drug use were not compared between cohorts.

outcomes.instruments: Subjective Opiate Withdrawal Scale (SOWS; 16 items, 0 to 64) and Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS; 11 items, 0 to 48) four times daily; severity categories for each; individual symptoms; heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, pupil diameter (pupillometer); tachycardia defined as heart rate above 100 beats a minute at least once.
outcomes.validity_norms: Both scales are standard published instruments. The SOWS categories are given as mild 1 to 10, moderate 11 to 20 and severe 21 to 30, which leaves scores above 30 on the 0 to 64 scale without a category.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary outcomes: each day's peak total SOWS and COWS score, and the percentage of participants in each severity category per day.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (alpha 0.05 throughout). The 35 counts the two total scores and their category analyses, 16 SOWS items, 11 COWS items, heart rate, two blood-pressure measures, pupil diameter and tachycardia, each with several model terms.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None. Self-ratings were made by participants who knew their own drug history; the authors state that COWS observers were not necessarily blind to fentanyl exposure.

analysis.effect_sizes: No standardized effect sizes, confidence intervals or between-group mean differences for the total scores are reported; daily means of total scores are in a supplementary table that was not read. Reported: SOWS model F(1,6) = 12.44, p < 0.01, with higher peak scores in the Fentanyl group on stabilization days 2 to 6 (text) or 2 to 5 (abstract); COWS model F(1,6) = 7.76, p < 0.001, higher on days 2 to 7 (text) or 2 to 6 (abstract). Proportion rating severe self-reported withdrawal, Fentanyl against Non-Fentanyl: day 2, 48% against 16%; day 3, 47% against 8%; day 4, 37% against 6%; day 5, 27% against 6%. Observer-rated mild withdrawal: day 2, 73% against 33%; day 3, 70% against 13%; day 4, 73% against 18%; day 5, 60% against 15%; day 6, 53% against 18%; day 7, 40% against 14%; no one reached moderately severe or severe COWS scores. Tachycardia at least once 43% against 19%, p < 0.05. Heart rate study-by-time interaction p = 0.007; diastolic pressure interaction p = 0.022; smaller pupils in the Fentanyl group on all days (study effect p < 0.001).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Both parent trials are registered (NCT01188421, NCT04325659); this secondary comparison has no registered protocol or analysis plan.
analysis.selective_reporting: Many outcomes without correction. The abstract and the Results disagree about the days on which the groups differed, and one sentence attributes a study effect to systolic pressure inside the diastolic-pressure paragraph (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not addressed; the authors note the small Fentanyl group (30) may limit power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: On the same fixed morphine regimen, the 30 people who entered with fentanyl exposure rated their withdrawal higher than the 103 who entered with non-fentanyl opioids a decade earlier on most stabilization days after the first, with ratings that rose to a peak early in the week and then eased, while the earlier cohort's ratings fell steadily from the first day. Severe self-rated withdrawal was 3 to 6 times as common on days 2 to 5; observers rated most of the Fentanyl group as mildly withdrawn and almost none in either group above moderate. Tachycardia was more common (43% against 19%). Similar first-day ratings in both groups.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors call these data the first empirical demonstration that fentanyl exposure produces more severe and sustained withdrawal, and conclude that withdrawal remained elevated despite morphine and concomitant medicines and took more than seven days to remit. Gaps: (1) causal wording from a non-randomized comparison with a historical cohort, different parent trials, an age difference, unblinded ratings and no adjustment; the authors list most of these limits but the abstract does not; (2) the outcome is withdrawal during fixed morphine substitution, so the finding is that this morphine regimen suppressed withdrawal less well in the fentanyl cohort, as the abstract also says, not a description of untreated fentanyl withdrawal; (3) 'more than seven days to remit' conflicts with the Results, where self-rated scores returned to the earlier cohort's level by day 7, and measurement stopped at day 7; (4) concomitant medicines were available only to the Fentanyl cohort, which would narrow rather than widen the difference in symptoms but complicates the vital-sign comparison; (5) suggestions about short-term opioid bridging and cimetidine go beyond the data.

timeline.event: Dunn et al. trial of extended-release tramadol for opioid withdrawal, the parent trial of the Non-Fentanyl cohort (as cited by this paper).
Luba et al. and Thakrar et al. on fentanyl withdrawal severity, body mass index and urine fentanyl concentration (as cited by this paper; not read).
This comparison (online November 2024).

replication.where_it_stands: A single, small, historically controlled comparison from one research unit. It is consistent with clinical reports that fentanyl withdrawal is harder to control with standard opioid regimens, but no study with a contemporaneous comparison group or adjustment for confounding has confirmed it in the papers read for this card.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grants R01DA018125, R01DA048761 and T32DA007209.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit (the first author also at Friends Research Institute, Baltimore); the same group ran both parent trials.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study enrolling people with fentanyl-positive and fentanyl-negative urine at the same time and place, testing all urine by chromatography for fentanyl, xylazine and nitazenes, recording amount and recency of use and body mass index, rating withdrawal blind to exposure, adjusting for age and other drug use, and following withdrawal both under a standard medicine regimen and after it ends.

domains.domain: Bias due to confounding
domains.note: Cohorts about a decade apart from different parent trials with different diagnostic criteria and age limits; the Fentanyl group was five years older; no adjustment; era-related changes in the supply (xylazine, nitazenes) and in the population cannot be separated from fentanyl exposure.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Exposure defined by a single entry urine test; non-fentanyl status confirmed by chromatography in only 3 of 103; amount, recency and co-use (including heroin within the Fentanyl group) not measured.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Volunteers for residential research trials in two eras; the Fentanyl cohort is the first 30 of an ongoing trial; selection into each trial may relate to withdrawal experience.

domains.domain: Bias due to post-exposure interventions
domains.note: Concomitant medicines for withdrawal symptoms (including clonazepam, loperamide and trazodone) were available only in the Fentanyl trial, introduced because withdrawal was uncontrolled; they could change symptoms and vital signs differently in the two groups.

domains.domain: Bias due to missing data
domains.note: The number contributing ratings on each day and any departures during the stabilization week are not reported.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Self-ratings by participants aware of their own drug history; observers not necessarily blind to fentanyl exposure, as the authors state.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Secondary analysis without a registered plan; about 35 outcomes without correction; the abstract and the Results give different day ranges for the group differences.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two domains are high (confounding by era, trial and age with no adjustment; concomitant medicines available to one cohort only), so the overall judgment is high. The direction of the main difference is unlikely to be produced by the concomitant medicines, which would narrow it, but confounding by era and supply could plausibly produce or enlarge it. The paper may be cited as one small historically controlled comparison showing more self-rated and observer-rated withdrawal, and more tachycardia, in a fentanyl-exposed cohort under the same fixed morphine regimen; it should not be cited as showing that fentanyl causes worse withdrawal, for the course of untreated fentanyl withdrawal, or for any effect size.

key_findings.finding: 133 participants: 103 in the Non-Fentanyl cohort (2010 to 2015) and 30 in the Fentanyl cohort (2021 to February 2024); 56% Black or African American, 84% men; the Fentanyl cohort was older (mean 46.0, SD 10.1, against 41.2, SD 10.2; p = 0.021), with no other significant demographic difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Participants, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Peak self-rated withdrawal (SOWS) differed by cohort, day and cohort-by-day (model F(1,6) = 12.44, p < 0.01): the Fentanyl cohort scored higher on stabilization days 2 to 6, with an inverted-U course peaking on day 2 and returning to the earlier cohort's level by day 7, while the Non-Fentanyl cohort declined steadily from day 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-Reported Withdrawal (SOWS) › Total Peak Scores, 1st paragraph; Figure 1A legend
key_findings.note: The abstract gives days 2 to 5 for the self-rated difference.

key_findings.finding: Severe self-rated withdrawal was more common in the Fentanyl cohort on day 2 (48% against 16%), day 3 (47% against 8%), day 4 (37% against 6%) and day 5 (27% against 6%); mild ratings were less common (for example day 2, 17% against 58%); days 1 and 7 did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-Reported Withdrawal (SOWS) › Withdrawal Categorical Ratings, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: No single symptom drove the difference: anxiety, sweating, tearing, runny nose, goosebumps, shaking, hot and cold flushes, bone and muscle aches, restlessness, nausea, vomiting, twitching and stomach cramps all showed cohort, day and interaction effects; yawning and the urge to use showed only day and interaction effects. For example, mean anxiety (0 to 4) on day 2 was 2.1 (SD 1.3) in the Fentanyl cohort against 0.9 (SD 1.0).
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-Reported Withdrawal (SOWS) › Individual Symptom Ratings, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Peak observer-rated withdrawal (COWS) differed by cohort, day and interaction (F(1,6) = 7.76, p < 0.001), higher in the Fentanyl cohort on days 2 to 7 and peaking on days 2 and 3. No participant reached moderately severe or severe COWS scores; the proportion with mild observer-rated withdrawal was higher in the Fentanyl cohort on days 2 to 7 (for example day 3, 70% against 13%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Observed Withdrawal (COWS) › Total Peak Scores, 1st paragraph; Withdrawal Categorical Ratings, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The abstract gives days 2 to 6 for the observer-rated difference.

key_findings.finding: Tachycardia (heart rate above 100 at least once) occurred in 43% of the Fentanyl cohort against 19% (p < 0.05); heart rate rose more steeply over the week in the Fentanyl cohort (interaction p = 0.007). Diastolic pressure showed a cohort-by-day interaction (p = 0.022). Pupils were smaller in the Fentanyl cohort on every day (cohort effect p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Physiological Measures › Heart Rate, 1st paragraph; Blood Pressure, 1st paragraph; Pupil Diameter, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Concomitant medicines for withdrawal symptoms were made available during stabilization in the Fentanyl trial only, because of a pattern of uncontrolled withdrawal; none were provided in the Non-Fentanyl trial.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Concomitant Medications, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations the decade between cohorts, morphine's possibly poor fit for stabilizing people exposed to fentanyl, incomplete urine confirmation in the earlier cohort, possible xylazine in the local fentanyl supply, observers not necessarily blind to exposure, the small Fentanyl group, and possible other synthetic opioids such as nitazenes.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the groups differed on stabilization days 2 to 5 (self-rated) and 2 to 6 (observer-rated); the Results give days 2 to 6 and days 2 to 7.
reporting_issues.consequence: The duration of the difference is uncertain by a day at each end; the Results text is the more detailed source.

reporting_issues.issue: The same F statistic with one set of degrees of freedom is printed for different model terms with different p values (for heart rate, F(1,6) = 16.12 with p < 0.001 for day, p = 0.007 for the interaction and p = 0.416 for cohort; similarly for blood pressure and pupil diameter), and F(1,6) cannot be the degrees of freedom for a repeated-measures model in 133 people over 7 days.
reporting_issues.consequence: The test statistics appear to be an overall model statistic repeated for each term; only the p values can be used, and they cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: In the diastolic blood-pressure paragraph, a significant cohort effect is attributed to systolic pressure (p = 0.003), although the systolic paragraph reports no cohort effect (p = 0.504); the same paragraph describes the Fentanyl group's diastolic interaction as a steeper increase in heart rate.
reporting_issues.consequence: Copy errors; the cohort effect probably concerns diastolic pressure, but this cannot be confirmed without the supplementary table.

reporting_issues.issue: The SOWS severity categories (mild 1 to 10, moderate 11 to 20, severe 21 to 30) do not cover scores from 31 to 64.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear how scores above 30 were categorized; presumably as severe.

reporting_issues.issue: Tachycardia is defined as heart rate above 100 at least once (Methods) but reported as more than one incidence (Results).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 43% and 19% may use either definition.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that withdrawal took more than seven days to remit, while the Results report that self-rated scores returned to the earlier cohort's level by day 7, and data collection ended at day 7.
reporting_issues.consequence: Remission after day 7 was not measured; the statement extrapolates beyond the data.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC12429306 (author manuscript; all sections, Tables 1 and 2, figure legends, acknowledgements, conflict statement, trial registrations and contributor information read; Figures 1 to 3 are images and their values were not extracted; the supplementary eTables 1 to 4, a Word file, were not opened)

design_detail: Review of news media reports (a content analysis of news articles), published under the journal's Editorial heading, without an abstract or section headings. A team of five reviewers searched LexisNexis for English-language print and online lay publications on first responder opioid exposure published in North America from January 2012 to March 2018. Articles were randomly assigned to one of the five reviewers, who used a standardized data collection form; articles that did not mention a specific case of first responder exposure were set aside; for each article reporting an exposure, the reviewer recorded the route of exposure, the documented clinical manifestations and whether any confirmatory drug testing was described. An exposure counted as confirmed only when an article described all three of a plausible exposure pathway, convincing symptoms and confirmatory laboratory testing. The search terms, the form, definitions of the three criteria and any second reading are not reported. The unit of analysis is the article; the number of distinct incidents is not reported. Results are three counts, one quarterly bar chart (Fig. 1) and two narrated examples; the rest of the text is commentary. Filed as a case series of media-reported incidents and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for case series without a comparison (as for the news study sc_forsyth_2012). No statistics.
can_establish: That among 214 English-language North American news articles (January 2012 to March 2018, found in LexisNexis) that described a specific first responder opioid exposure, the reviewers found none that described a plausible route, symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity and confirmatory laboratory testing together; that only one incident, reported in two newspapers, mentioned any laboratory test of an exposed responder, a urine result described as traces of opiates, which the authors judge unlikely to have come from a test able to detect fentanyl; and that such articles were few before 2016 and peaked in the second and third quarters of 2017.
cannot_establish: Whether any responder was or was not poisoned by an opioid (news text, not medical, police or laboratory records, was examined, and testing was almost never reported); how many distinct incidents there were (articles were counted, and one incident can appear in several); how often a route, a particular symptom, naloxone or hospital transport was reported (only the three-way combination is given); or that the reports caused symptoms through a nocebo effect, unnecessary protective equipment or delays in care, which the authors put forward without testing them.

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: news articles found by a LexisNexis search for English-language print and online lay publications on first responder opioid exposure published in North America between January 2012 and March 2018 (p. 112, 5th paragraph). The counts are nested: 1408 retrieved, 1016 judged relevant, 214 describing a specific exposure (pp. 112–113, 6th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: articles in the search period and region that described a specific case of first responder opioid exposure. Set aside: articles that discussed the issue without a specific case (editors' calculation: 1016 − 214 = 802). Excluded as not relevant, without stated reasons (editors' calculation): 392 of 1408. The search terms and the LexisNexis sources searched are not reported.
sample.demographics: Not reported, either for the articles (outlets, countries, dates beyond the quarter of publication) or for the responders described (police, EMS or fire; number per incident). The two narrated incidents involved police officers in Canada (Montreal, 2013; British Columbia, 2016) (p. 113).
sample.selection_effects: The 214 are the media's selection, which is the object of study: incidents that reached English-language print or online news indexed by LexisNexis. Social media posts are outside the stated frame and broadcast coverage is not mentioned. Repeat coverage is not separated from distinct incidents, so heavily covered incidents count several times.

exposure.measurement: The exposure is what each news article said about an incident: the route, the clinical manifestations and any confirmatory drug testing, abstracted by one reviewer per article on a standardized form (p. 112, 5th paragraph). Nothing was checked against medical, police or laboratory records.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Amounts were not recorded. Routes as reported in the articles were recorded, but their distribution is not reported; the routes of concern raised in 2016 were small amounts of drug on patients' clothing and drug in the air (p. 112, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: which drugs the incidents involved (fentanyl, analogues or other opioids) is not tabulated. The first article concerned an illicit facility making drugs including desmethylfentanyl (p. 113, 7th paragraph).

comparison.controls: None. Reported symptoms were judged against the reviewers' understanding of opioid toxicity without a stated definition. The text names suppressed breathing as how opioids kill (p. 112, 1st paragraph) and respiratory depression as a symptom of opioid poisoning (p. 114, 17th paragraph, item 5), and judges the narrated cases' racing heart and rash (2013) and nausea, dizziness and raised heart rate and blood pressure (2016) not consistent with exposure (p. 113). No comparison set of articles (for example, reports of other occupational exposures) was examined.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to news articles; nothing is known about the health, anxiety or earlier experiences of the responders described.

outcomes.instruments: A standardized data collection form (not published) recording, per article, the route of exposure, the documented clinical manifestations and whether confirmatory drug testing was described (p. 112, 5th paragraph); a confirmation rule requiring all three of a plausible exposure pathway, convincing symptoms and confirmatory laboratory testing (pp. 112–113, 6th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No definitions of a plausible pathway, convincing symptoms or confirmatory testing are given beyond the examples in the text; the form was not piloted or validated as far as reported; no inter-rater agreement is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: A confirmed exposure is an article describing all three elements. A test was judged non-confirmatory when it could not detect fentanyl (an opiate screen) or could not show acute exposure (urine tests detect exposure over the last several days) (p. 113, 10th paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive counts, no statistical tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable in the usual sense. Each article was read by one randomly assigned reviewer, with no duplicate reading or adjudication described, and the authors began from the view that the scientific literature held no confirmation of such exposures (p. 112, 5th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: No statistics. Counts: 1408 articles retrieved, 1016 relevant (editors' calculation: 72%), 214 describing a specific exposure (21% of the relevant), 0 of 214 meeting all three confirmation criteria; one incident, in two newspapers, with any mention of laboratory testing of an exposed person (editors' calculation: two of 214 articles, 0.9%). Editors' reading of Fig. 1 (unlabelled bars measured against the gridlines): 1 article in 2013 Q2, 1 in 2015 Q2, 6, 11 and 13 in 2016 Q2 to Q4, 9 in 2017 Q1, 76 in 2017 Q2, 64 in 2017 Q3, 24 in 2017 Q4 and 9 in 2018 Q1, summing to 214; about 140 (65%) in the second and third quarters of 2017. A confidence interval for the zero count would be misleading, because articles cluster by incident and the number of incidents is unknown.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the three-way combination is reported; counts for each criterion (articles reporting a route, symptoms judged consistent, naloxone, hospital transport) are not, and the text uses most and many without numbers (pp. 113–114). The number of distinct incidents, the search terms, the data collection form and the reasons for excluding 392 articles are not given. Two incidents are narrated: the first reported and the only one with any testing.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 214 news articles describing specific first responder opioid exposures (January 2012 to March 2018), the reviewers found none describing a plausible route, opioid-consistent symptoms and confirmatory testing together; only one incident (two articles) mentioned a laboratory test, an opiate urine result that, as the authors explain, probably came from an opiate screen, which does not detect fentanyl, and could not show acute exposure. The articles clustered in mid-2017. Because each article was coded by one reviewer against undefined criteria and only the combination is reported, the data show above all that the news reports did not describe confirmation, not what happened to the responders.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The text concludes that the phenomenon reported in the news has not been confirmed scientifically (p. 112, 3rd paragraph) and that “analysis of lay media reports is consistent with the consensus of the medical community” that poisoning of responders from incidental contact is extremely unlikely (p. 114, 18th paragraph); consistency is a fair description of what absent reports of confirmation can show. Statements that go beyond the data: that in most cases the responders had real symptoms which they attributed to opioids (no count; pp. 113–114, 14th paragraph); that lay media reports are the only evidence of the phenomenon, which rests on no described literature search (p. 113, 11th paragraph); that regulatory agencies recommended unnecessary protective equipment (p. 113, 11th paragraph) and that unnecessary equipment delays care (p. 112, 4th paragraph; p. 114, 16th paragraph; citing ref 4), neither examined by the review; and that unverified reports plausibly contribute to illness through a nocebo effect, extrapolated from experiments with sham Wi-Fi signals (p. 114, 15th paragraph).

timeline.event: First news article in this review describing a responder exposure (Montreal Gazette, 14 May 2013): officers in an illicit drug facility, one taken to hospital with heart problems and three with rashes; no testing described (p. 113).

September: a DEA warning that fentanyl can be absorbed through the skin or inhaled, quoted from a trade-magazine article (p. 112, ref 6); the British Columbia incident, the only one in this review with any laboratory test mentioned (p. 113).

June: a DEA video advising against touching fentanyl without protective equipment, shown with level A equipment (p. 112, ref 7). News articles on responder exposures peak in the second and third quarters (Fig. 1, p. 113).

December: the ACMT and AACT position statement on preventing occupational fentanyl exposure of emergency responders, described here as the first scientific guidance on the low likelihood of exposure (p. 113, ref 8).

NIOSH Health Hazard Evaluation of two officers who fell ill after powder blew into their faces: no laboratory testing of the officers, and no fentanyl or other opioid identified in the seized substances (card sc_niosh_2018).

Chiu et al., two NIOSH case investigations among law enforcement officers (Am J Ind Med 62(5):439–447), cited here as finding manifestations not consistent with opioids and no officer tested positive for opioid metabolites (p. 112, ref 9); not read.
This review: none of 214 news articles (January 2012 to March 2018) described a confirmed exposure.
Beletsky et al., an analysis of misinformation about overdose risk from casual contact with fentanyl in mainstream and social media (card by another reader; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: No repetition of this media review is reported in the paper. Its central point, that the news reports did not document confirmed exposures, agrees with the one field investigation read for this project (NIOSH 2018), in which officers who fell ill were not tested and no opioid was identified in the seized drugs. The pharmacological basis for judging poisoning from incidental contact very unlikely comes from the ACMT–AACT position statement the authors cite, not from this review.

Published under the Editorial heading in the Journal of Medical Toxicology (copyright American College of Medical Toxicology), with a named supervising editor; received 24 January, revised 29 January, accepted 2 February and published online 24 February 2020; the review process is not described (p. 112). The senior author, A. I. D-2); the editorial cites that statement with six names and et al. (ref 8, p. 114). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For the clinical question: prospective surveillance of suspected occupational exposures among responders, with a standardized assessment at first contact (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, pupil size, level of consciousness), blood sampled within hours and analysed by mass spectrometry for fentanyl, its analogues and the other drugs present, and laboratory analysis of the material contacted. For the media question: a content analysis with published search terms and coding definitions, two coders per article with agreement statistics, incidents de-duplicated across articles, and each incident checked against medical or laboratory records.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: LexisNexis English-language print and online news for North America fits the target (lay media reports), but the sources searched and the search terms are not given; social media is outside the frame and broadcast coverage is not mentioned.

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled appropriately
domains.note: All retrieved articles were screened, but 392 of 1408 were excluded as not relevant without stated reasons, and 802 relevant articles without a specific case were set aside (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 3. Adequate sample size
domains.note: 214 articles, but the number of distinct incidents, the unit that matters for the question, is not reported; one incident appeared in two newspapers.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The articles and incidents are described only by quarter of publication (Fig. 1) and two narrated examples; outlets, countries, responder types, routes and symptoms are not tabulated.

domains.note: A standardized form and random allocation of articles to five reviewers, but each article coded by one reviewer, with no inter-rater agreement and an unpublished form.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for case series without a comparison and as for the news study sc_forsyth_2012; the commentary that makes up most of the editorial is described, not appraised. The editors summarise the risk of bias as moderate for what the count describes, whether news articles reported a confirmed exposure: the zero rests on unstated criteria applied by one reviewer per article, but it follows mainly from the near-total absence of reported testing (one incident), which is hard to misclassify. The larger limitation is indirectness: news text cannot show whether responders were or were not exposed or poisoned. The paper may be cited for: the search frame and counts (1408 retrieved, 1016 relevant, 214 describing an exposure, none confirmed); the single incident with any laboratory test and the authors' explanation of why an opiate urine screen could not detect fentanyl or show acute exposure; the timing of the articles (few before 2016, a peak in mid-2017; quarterly values only as the editors' reading of Fig. 1); and, as the authors' view, their call for journalists to check for confirmatory testing and seek expert input. It may not be cited for the number of incidents, for the share of reported symptoms consistent or inconsistent with opioid toxicity, as evidence that no responder was ever poisoned, or for the nocebo, protective-equipment and delayed-care claims, which it did not test.

key_findings.finding: Method: a team of five reviewers searched LexisNexis for English-language print and online lay publications on first responder opioid exposure published in North America between January 2012 and March 2018; articles were randomly assigned to one of the five reviewers, who used a standardized data collection form; articles not mentioning a specific case of first responder exposure were set aside; for each reported exposure the reviewer recorded the route, the documented clinical manifestations and whether any confirmatory drug testing was described.

key_findings.finding: Finding text unchanged. Corrected note: Editors' calculation: 72% of retrieved articles were relevant; 21% of relevant articles (214 of 1016) described a specific exposure; 802 relevant articles discussed the issue without a specific case. No separate counts are given for the route and symptom criteria; for testing, the text reports only one incident, described in two newspapers, with any mention of laboratory testing (p. 113, 9th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: The first article describing a responder exposure appeared on 14 May 2013; there were few until 2016, when reports resumed, and a spike in the second and third quarters of 2017 (Fig. 1, a quarterly bar chart of media-reported first responder opioid exposures). Editors' reading of the chart's axis and unlabelled bars: quarters from 2013 Q1 to 2018 Q1; 1 in 2013 Q2, 1 in 2015 Q2, 6, 11 and 13 in 2016 Q2 to Q4, 9 in 2017 Q1, 76 in 2017 Q2, 64 in 2017 Q3, 24 in 2017 Q4 and 9 in 2018 Q1, a total of 214, about 140 (65%) of them in 2017 Q2 and Q3.

key_findings.note: Values are not printed: the chart is an embedded image, and bar heights were measured in pixels against the 10-unit gridlines on a 300-dpi rendering, each reading within 0.3 of a whole number. Their sum equals the 214 articles, so the bars count articles (repeat coverage included), although the chart is labelled exposures.

key_findings.finding: The first article (Montreal Gazette, 14 May 2013) described officers entering an illicit Canadian facility that made drugs including desmethylfentanyl: one officer was taken to hospital with heart problems, and three others, who had handled drugs wearing masks and gloves, developed rashes on their arms. The authors judge that neither a racing heart nor a rash is a symptom of opioid toxicity; no confirmatory testing was described.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Only one incident, described on 14 September 2016 in two British Columbia newspapers, mentioned laboratory testing of an exposed person: an officer assisting an unconscious young man in a car smelled a chemical odour and became nauseated and dizzy; hospital tests showed raised heart rate and blood pressure, and traces of opiates in his urine. The authors explain that opiate screens identify codeine, morphine and heroin but not fentanyl or its analogues, that fentanyl immunoassays were not commercially available for clinical use in 2016, and that a positive urine test shows exposure within the last several days rather than acute exposure; they judge that the report has no plausible route, no consistent symptoms and no well-described laboratory confirmation.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 9th and 10th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The date differs from one of the two cited newspaper reports (ref 11 is dated 16 September 2016, ref 12 14 September 2016; p. 114).

key_findings.finding: The authors state that in most cases the responders had real symptoms that they attributed to an opioid exposure, and that the writer reported this as fact; that symptoms such as a rapid heart rate or rash are not consistent with opioid toxicity and may have other causes, including psychological stress or skin irritation from protective equipment; that many responders were given naloxone or taken to hospital as a precaution; and that, because of patient privacy, stories said a responder was treated for opioid exposure without input from the treating physician that the treatment was precautionary and did not confirm exposure.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 14th paragraph (p. 113, right column, continuing on p. 114)
key_findings.note: No counts are given for most or many; the share of articles reporting naloxone, hospital transport or each symptom cannot be recovered.

key_findings.finding: Second-hand: the authors cite a rare peer-reviewed case report of opioid exposure among law enforcement officers in which the clinical manifestations were not consistent with opioids and none of the officers tested was positive for opioid metabolites (ref 9, Chiu et al., Am J Ind Med 2019).
key_findings.locator: Running text, 3rd paragraph (p. 112, left column, continuing in the right column); reference 9 (p. 114)
key_findings.note: Chiu et al. (2019) was not read; its DOI is not printed in the editorial.

key_findings.finding: Background as stated: in 2016 commenters on an online forum of medical toxicologists raised unverified reports that responders could be harmed by small amounts of drug on patients' clothing or in the air; in September 2016 the DEA warned that fentanyl can be absorbed through the skin or by accidental inhalation of airborne powder (quoted from a trade-magazine article, ref 6); and a June 2017 DEA video advised not touching fentanyl without proper protective equipment, shown with level A equipment, a positive-pressure suit with self-contained breathing apparatus (ref 7).
key_findings.locator: Running text, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that, because the scientific literature contains no confirmed responder exposures, lay media reports remain the only 'evidence' of the phenomenon (quotation marks theirs); that, as a result of these and other media reports and despite experts' view that standard gloves suffice in most cases, regulatory agencies recommended protective equipment the authors call unnecessary and manufacturers advertised products to EMS to protect against skin absorption of fentanyl (refs 6, 14); and that the ACMT-AACT position statement, which they date to December 2017, was the first scientific guidance on the low likelihood of exposure, leaving six months in which unvalidated reports went unchallenged in scientific journals. Note: No literature search is described for the statement that the scientific literature holds no confirmed exposure. The causal link to media reports is the authors' assertion, not examined. The position statement was published online on 25 August 2017 (Moss et al., 2017, PDF p. 1); December 2017 is its issue date (ref 8), so the six-month gap is counted from the issue.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 11th and 13th paragraphs
key_findings.note: No literature search is described for the statement that the scientific literature holds no confirmed exposure.

key_findings.finding: Hypotheses offered without testing: by analogy with experiments in which people shown news stories about health effects of Wi-Fi reported tactile symptoms under sham Wi-Fi signals (refs 17, 18), unverified reports of opioid exposure may contribute to illness among responders through a nocebo effect; and delayed rescue breathing and naloxone, with the discomfort and slower performance caused by extra protective equipment (ref 4), may be the greatest danger of responders' fear of exposure.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 15th and 16th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the authors state that the 2017 ACMT-AACT conclusions still hold (unintentional exposure is unlikely because opioids are poorly absorbed through the skin and unlikely to be in the air; standard nitrile gloves during patient contact; a mask only in the unlikely case that drug is in the air; powder on the skin removed with soap and water; naloxone reserved for patients with symptoms of opioid poisoning such as respiratory depression). They call for news stories on suspected exposures to attempt to determine whether confirmatory testing was done, to include an expert's view on whether the symptoms fit opioid poisoning and to describe the physical properties of opioids, and they conclude that the analysis is consistent with the medical consensus that unintentional poisoning of responders from incidental contact is extremely unlikely.
key_findings.locator: Running text, 17th paragraph with its numbered list, and 18th paragraph (continuing in the right column)

design_detail: Joint position statement of the American College of Medical Toxicology (ACMT) and the American Academy of Clinical Toxicology (AACT) on the risk to emergency responders (law enforcement, emergency medical services) from incidental contact with fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, and on protective equipment, decontamination and naloxone. Who wrote it: eight authors (affiliations under funding), who performed the literature search and drafted the statement for the two bodies. On what evidence: by the statement's own account, the opinion and clinical experience of an ACMT task force of members, together with a literature search for which no databases, dates, search terms or selection rules are given; the draft was reviewed by the ACMT Position Statement and Guidelines Committee, the ACMT Board of Directors and the whole College membership, revised by the task force, and approved by the ACMT Board of Directors and the AACT Board of Trustees (PDF p. 2, Methodology). Received 2 August 2017, accepted 10 August 2017; whether it was peer reviewed outside the two organizations is not stated. The evidence offered is pharmacokinetic and physical-chemical reasoning (fentanyl patch absorption, inhalational bioavailability, industrial occupational exposure limits, vapour pressure) with two worked estimates for fentanyl, one case report of a splash to the face, one animal study on naloxone and carfentanil, and US agency warnings and news reports about responders' symptoms. No new data. Filed as narrative-review (a professional bodies' position paper) and appraised with the editors' narrative-review checklist, as the round brief directs.
can_establish: What two North American clinical-toxicology bodies concluded in August 2017 about responders' risk from incidental contact with fentanyl and its analogues, and the pharmacokinetic reasoning and worked estimates for fentanyl on which they based it.
cannot_establish: How often responders are actually exposed or poisoned (no case series, surveillance data or measured blood levels are presented, and the absence of confirmed cases is the authors' observation without a search record or denominator), whether the fentanyl estimates hold for more potent analogues such as carfentanil (none is calculated), or how well gloves and respirators perform (not tested).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (position statement; no participants and no data collection).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria for the literature search are stated (PDF p. 2, Methodology). The statement cites 31 references: pharmacology and pharmacokinetic papers (fentanyl patches, inhaled fentanyl, a 1987 volunteer study of skin absorption of fentanyl and sufentanil), a fentanyl patch product label, an occupational-exposure study of pharmaceutical workers, a vapour-pressure study, one case report (a veterinarian splashed with carfentanil), one animal study (naloxone after carfentanil in wapiti), an analysis of the 2002 Moscow theatre casualties, a review of opioid overdose management, US agency web pages (DEA, NIOSH) and an MMWR report, two news reports and an emergency-medicine news column (PDF pp. 4–5).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the task force. No study of responders' exposures, symptoms or toxicology is cited: the responder incidents appear only through the DEA warning and two news reports, and the statement characterizes them as nonspecific without examining them case by case (PDF p. 2). One cited review on transdermal fentanyl (ref. 20, Nelson and Schwaner, 2009) appears to be co-authored by one of the authors (Lewis S. Nelson).

exposure.measurement: Not measured. Exposure scenarios are reasoned, not observed: skin contact (fentanyl patch absorption data used as an upper bound), inhalation of airborne particles (inhalational bioavailability and industrial occupational exposure limits), splashes to the eyes and mouth (one case report) and mere proximity (vapour pressure) (PDF pp. 2–3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: The statement's worked estimates, reported as conditions of its own arithmetic and not as guidance: a reference amount of 100 mcg of fentanyl; both palms covered with fentanyl patches delivering 2.5 mcg/cm2/h at steady state (body surface 17,000 cm2, palm 0.5%) would take about 14 minutes to deliver it; at the highest airborne concentration encountered by industrial workers, an unprotected person would need nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 mcg (concentration, breathing volume and bioavailability not stated, nor whether the dose is inhaled or absorbed) (PDF p. 2). Why 100 mcg is the reference amount is not explained.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, except in the case report, where the splash contained carfentanil with xylazine and the authors say it is unclear how far the drowsiness was due to carfentanil (PDF p. 3).

comparison.controls: None (no data). The statement positions itself against earlier guidance it describes: a June 2016 DEA warning that cautioned against field-testing suspected fentanyl and recommended gloves and a mask during testing, and a NIOSH bulletin that, citing an absence of empirical evidence, recommended a P100-rated respirator, nitrile gloves and eye protection, with coveralls or sleeves for tasks that could aerosolize the drug (PDF p. 2).

outcomes.instruments: None. The outcome discussed is clinically significant opioid toxicity, identified by objective signs (respiratory depression, hypoventilation, depressed level of consciousness), as distinct from nonspecific symptoms such as dizziness or anxiety (PDF pp. 1–2).
outcomes.operationalization: Poisoning means objective signs of opioid toxicity; responders' reported symptoms without such signs are treated as not consistent with opioid toxicity (PDF pp. 1–2). Risk is judged by comparing the time needed to take up 100 mcg of fentanyl through the skin, or to reach a dose of 100 mcg by breathing contaminated air, with the time available to remove the drug.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The quantitative content is the statement's own arithmetic (skin: about 14 minutes to 100 mcg of fentanyl with both palms covered by patches; inhalation: nearly 200 minutes to 100 mcg at the highest airborne concentration encountered by workers) and parameters cited from other sources: inhalational bioavailability of fentanyl 12–100%; patches take 3–13 h to reach a therapeutic serum concentration and 35 h to peak; vapour pressure of fentanyl 4.6 × 10^-6 Pa; time-weighted occupational exposure limits of 1 (alfentanil), 0.1 (fentanyl) and 0.032 (sufentanil) mcg/m3; absorption of fentanyl across mucous membranes more than 30-fold that across skin (PDF pp. 2–3). Editors' check of the skin estimate: 2 × 0.5% × 17,000 cm2 = 170 cm2; 170 cm2 × 2.5 mcg/cm2/h = 425 mcg/h; 100 mcg takes about 14 minutes, so the figure assumes 0.5% of body surface per palm. The inhalation estimate cannot be reproduced because its inputs are not given.
analysis.selective_reporting: No search record, so the completeness of the cited evidence cannot be judged. The inhalation estimate is given without its inputs. No calculation is given for carfentanil or any other analogue, although the conclusions and recommendations cover them.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A consensus of two clinical-toxicology bodies supported by pharmacokinetic reasoning: skin absorption of fentanyl is slow even from patches designed to deliver it (about 14 minutes for 100 mcg with both palms covered, by the statement's arithmetic); powder or tablets on skin would be absorbed less and can be brushed or washed off; breathing the highest airborne concentration encountered by industrial workers would take nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 mcg (whether inhaled or absorbed is not stated); and fentanyl's very low vapour pressure is said to suggest that evaporation of standing product is not a practical concern. Mucous membranes are treated as a real route (more than 30-fold the absorption of skin; one case of drowsiness within 2 minutes after a carfentanil and xylazine splash to the eyes and mouth). The authors had seen no report of a responder with signs of opioid toxicity from incidental contact; the reports they describe were of nonspecific symptoms without objective signs.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The opening position calls the risk of clinically significant exposure 'extremely low', and the recommendations state as a fact that toxicity cannot occur from simply being near the drug (PDF pp. 1, 3). The statement itself says its recommendations are primarily consensus expert opinion because data are limited (PDF p. 3). Gaps: (1) the reassurance rests on calculation and on the absence of reports known to the authors, without a search record, a case series or a denominator of exposures; (2) both worked estimates are for fentanyl only and use a 100 mcg reference amount that is not justified, while carfentanil is described as 10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals and the recommendations extend to all analogues; (3) the inhalation estimate cannot be checked from the text; (4) the summary says an N95 respirator gives sufficient protection, while the recommendation section says an N95 or P100 is likely to give reasonable protection (PDF pp. 1, 3). A headline version such as 'touching fentanyl cannot hurt you' overstates the statement: it calls incidental skin absorption very unlikely to cause toxicity, still recommends nitrile gloves and washing with water, and treats splashes to the eyes and mouth as a real route. The opposite message, that fentanyl exposure kills (the title of the DEA warning cited as ref. 10), is not supported for incidental contact by any case the statement describes.

timeline.event: Moscow theatre siege: an aerosol suspected to contain carfentanil and remifentanil is used to subdue hostage-takers and 125 people die (ref. 16, as summarized in the statement, PDF p. 2); the statement uses this as its worst-case scenario for respiratory protection.

DEA warning to police and the public on fentanyl exposure (June 2016), and a NIOSH bulletin recommending a P100 respirator, nitrile gloves and eye protection while citing an absence of empirical evidence (refs 10 and 11, as described in the statement, PDF p. 2).
News reports of responders treated after possible exposures (Baltimore Sun; Global News, Winnipeg), cited by the statement for responders' concern (refs 12 and 13).
This joint ACMT and AACT position statement, published online 25 August 2017.

replication.where_it_stands: As of August 2017 the statement records no confirmed case of opioid toxicity in a responder from incidental contact and offers expert consensus and pharmacokinetic reasoning rather than exposure data. Cite it as the two bodies' position and reasoning. Later case series, toxicology studies of responders' reported exposures or other professional statements were not among this reader's files and are not appraised here.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective series of emergency responders reporting suspected incidental exposure, with objective clinical findings and blood toxicology taken soon after the event and the seized material analysed; and laboratory measurements of how much powdered fentanyl and carfentanil passes through skin, gloves and skin-cleaning steps in the first minutes of contact.

domains.domain: Systematic search and explicit selection
domains.note: A literature search is mentioned without databases, dates, terms or criteria; the evidence was chosen by the task force (PDF p. 2).

domains.domain: Appraisal of cited studies
domains.note: No formal appraisal. The statement acknowledges that data are limited and that the case report's drowsiness may not have been due to carfentanil, but the quantitative argument leans on a patch product label, a 1987 volunteer study and one animal study (wapiti) without discussing how directly they apply to powder on a responder's skin.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The cited evidence is almost all others' work; one review of transdermal fentanyl (ref. 20) appears to be co-authored by one of the authors.

domains.domain: Separation of evidence from speculation
domains.note: The recommendations are labelled as primarily consensus expert opinion (PDF p. 3), but the summary states several conclusions categorically (toxicity cannot occur from proximity; an N95 provides sufficient protection) that rest on calculation rather than measurement, and the inhalation estimate is given without inputs.

domains.domain: Balance of reassurance against hazard for responders
domains.note: The hazard side is set out (inhalational bioavailability up to 100%, mucosal absorption, the Moscow theatre deaths, the NIOSH recommendations) alongside the reassurance, but the responder incidents themselves are represented only by a DEA warning and news reports and are not examined; under-represented: case-level evidence on what happened to the responders, and any quantitative treatment of the more potent analogues.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument exists for a position statement (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. Who wrote it: eight authors drafting for an ACMT task force, with approval by the ACMT and AACT boards after College-wide review. On what evidence: opinion and clinical experience, pharmacokinetic parameters drawn mostly from fentanyl patch data and a product label, physical properties, industrial exposure limits, one case report and one animal study, from an undocumented literature search. Overall high because selection is unsystematic, and the overall judgment cannot be milder than the worst domain; within that, the skin estimate is explicit and checkable, and the statement is candid that it is expert opinion. Citable for: the two bodies' 2017 position and reasoning (skin absorption of fentanyl is slow and patch-based estimates are an upper bound; no confirmed responder toxicity from incidental contact known to the authors; objective signs, not vague symptoms, should prompt naloxone; recommended gloves, washing with water and respiratory protection for airborne powder). Not citable for: a measured rate of responder poisoning, the safety of contact with carfentanil or other analogues, or tested performance of gloves or respirators.

key_findings.finding: The ACMT and AACT position: the risk of clinically significant exposure for emergency responders is extremely low; the authors had seen no reports of responders developing signs or symptoms consistent with opioid toxicity from incidental contact with opioids; incidental skin absorption is unlikely to cause opioid toxicity; nitrile gloves give sufficient skin protection for routine handling, and, in exceptional circumstances where drug particles or droplets are suspended in the air, an N95 respirator gives sufficient protection; in the unlikely event of poisoning, the position reserves naloxone for objective signs of hypoventilation or a depressed level of consciousness, not vague concerns such as dizziness or anxiety; no persistent effects are expected without prolonged hypoxia. The statement presents these as the two bodies' positions at the time of writing, after a review of the issue and the literature, and says that individual practitioners may differ.
key_findings.locator: Opening position statement before Background, 2nd paragraph (both columns)

key_findings.finding: Responders' reported symptoms after contact were nonspecific (dizziness, a feeling of the body shutting down, a feeling of dying) and came without objective signs of opioid toxicity such as respiratory depression; the source cited for these reports is the June 2016 DEA warning (ref. 10), and two news reports are cited for responders' concern (refs 12 and 13).
key_findings.locator: Background, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: No case series, toxicology or clinical record of these incidents is presented.

key_findings.finding: Basis of the statement: the recommendations rest on the opinion and clinical experience of a task force of members plus a literature search (no databases, dates, terms or criteria stated), reviewed by the ACMT Position Statement and Guidelines Committee, the ACMT Board of Directors and the College membership, and approved by the ACMT Board of Directors and the AACT Board of Trustees; because data are limited, the recommendations are described as primarily consensus expert opinion.
key_findings.locator: Methodology (p. 2); Recommendations, 1st paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Skin: fentanyl patches take 3–13 h to produce a therapeutic serum concentration and 35 h to reach peak; the statement's worked example is that with both palms covered by fentanyl patches (body surface 17,000 cm2, palm 0.5%, steady-state delivery 2.5 mcg/cm2/h) absorbing 100 mcg would take about 14 minutes. The authors argue that this overestimates uptake from powder or tablets, which need moisture and dissolution and lack a patch's delivery matrix, and that the steady-state rate overstates absorption in the first minutes, when drug seen on skin can be brushed or washed off; toxicity from small unintentional skin exposures is therefore very unlikely and would not develop rapidly.
key_findings.locator: Dermal Exposure Risk for Fentanyl and Fentanyl Analogs, 1st–3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Editors' check: 2 × 0.5% × 17,000 cm2 × 2.5 mcg/cm2/h = 425 mcg/h, so 100 mcg in about 14 minutes; the estimate assumes 0.5% of body surface per palm. Why 100 mcg is the reference amount is not explained. A small volunteer study (ref. 25) found sufentanil absorbed through occluded forearm skin comparably to fentanyl, without determining bioavailability.

key_findings.finding: Inhalation: fentanyl's bioavailability by inhalation is described as potentially high (12–100%); industrial time-weighted occupational exposure limits are 1 mcg/m3 for alfentanil, 0.1 for fentanyl and 0.032 for sufentanil; at the highest airborne concentration encountered by workers, an unprotected person would need nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 mcg of fentanyl; fentanyl's very low vapour pressure (4.6 × 10^-6 Pa) is said to suggest that evaporation from standing product into a gas is not a practical concern.
key_findings.locator: Inhalation Exposure Risk for Fentanyl and Fentanyl Analogs, 1st–3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The airborne concentration, breathing volume and bioavailability behind the 200-minute estimate are not stated, nor whether the 100 mcg is the amount inhaled or the amount absorbed.

key_findings.finding: Worst case considered: an aerosol suspected to contain carfentanil and remifentanil was used to subdue hostage-takers in a Moscow theatre in 2002, and 125 people died; the authors judge an optimized airborne dispersal device unlikely in a local event but considered this scenario for respiratory protection.
key_findings.locator: Inhalation Exposure Risk for Fentanyl and Fentanyl Analogs, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The number of deaths is printed in words (one hundred twenty-five).

key_findings.finding: Eyes and mouth: fentanyl is absorbed more than 30-fold better across mucous membranes than across skin; in one case report, a healthy veterinarian splashed in the eyes and mouth with dart contents (1.5 mg carfentanil with 50 mg xylazine) became drowsy within 2 minutes despite washing his face at once and responded promptly to naltrexone; the authors say it is unclear how far the effects were due to carfentanil. Splash protection rated by OSHA is judged sufficient.
key_findings.locator: Ocular-Facial Exposure Risk for Fentanyl and Fentanyl Analogs, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Naloxone: information on naloxone reversal of fentanyl analogues in humans and animals is described as scant; anecdotal reports (an emergency-medicine news column, ref. 30) suggest higher-than-usual doses may be needed, while animal data (one study in wapiti, ref. 31) suggest standard doses should be sufficient for carfentanil. The statement also gives naloxone administration and airway-management recommendations, citing a clinical review (ref. 29); they are clinical guidance, not findings, and are not reproduced on this card.
key_findings.locator: Naloxone, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Naloxone Administration and Airway Management, bullet points (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Proximity and detection dogs: for toxicity to occur the drug must enter the blood and brain from the environment, and the statement holds that toxicity cannot occur from simply being near the drug; detection dogs may be poisoned, but their risk is not equivalent to humans' because of their different contact with the environment.
key_findings.locator: General Precautions and Management of Exposure, 2nd and 3rd bullet points

key_findings.finding: Skin precautions recommended: nitrile gloves for routine handling; water-resistant coveralls in enclosed spaces potentially heavily contaminated with a highly potent opioid; washing incidental skin exposure at once with water; no alcohol-based hand sanitizers, which the statement says do not wash opioids off and may increase absorption.
key_findings.locator: Dermal Precautions, three bullet points
key_findings.note: No reference is given for the statement about hand sanitizers.

key_findings.finding: Respiratory and other recommendations: in the unusual circumstance of significant airborne powder, a properly fitted N95 respirator or P100 mask is likely to give reasonable respiratory protection; OSHA-approved eye and face protection where a splash is possible; in the absence of prolonged hypoxia no persistent effects are expected, and people with small subclinical exposures or who awaken normally after naloxone will not have long-term effects.
key_findings.locator: Respiratory Precautions (p. 3); Mucous Membrane/Splash Exposure; Long-term Sequelae of Exposure (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Background figures cited from other sources: reported US mortality from synthetic opioids rose 72.2% (to 9850) from 2014 to 2015 (ref. 1), which the authors think undercounts deaths from analogues; fentanyl is 50–100 times as potent as morphine at the mu-opioid receptor, and carfentanil 10,000 times as potent as morphine in animals.
key_findings.locator: Background, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures; cite the primary sources for them.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary says an N95 respirator provides sufficient protection when drug particles or droplets are airborne (PDF p. 1), while the recommendation it summarizes says an N95 respirator or P100 mask is likely to provide reasonable protection in the unusual circumstance of significant airborne powder (PDF p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary states the respiratory recommendation more firmly than the section it summarizes; claims should use the recommendation's wording.

reporting_issues.issue: The inhalation estimate (nearly 200 minutes of exposure to reach a dose of 100 mcg of fentanyl) is given without the airborne concentration, breathing volume or bioavailability used, and without saying whether the dose is the amount inhaled or the amount absorbed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure cannot be reproduced; cite it as the authors' estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: No estimate is offered for carfentanil or any other analogue, although the statement gives carfentanil's potency as 10,000 times that of morphine in animals and extends its conclusions and recommendations to analogues.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reassurance about skin and airborne exposure is quantified for fentanyl only; for analogues it rests on the bodies' judgment.

reporting_issues.issue: The 100 mcg reference amount used in both worked estimates is not explained (for example, as an amount expected to cause toxicity in a person without opioid tolerance).
reporting_issues.consequence: The estimates show how slowly fentanyl is taken up, not how far a given exposure falls below a harmful amount.

reporting_issues.issue: The recommendation against alcohol-based hand sanitizers (said not to remove opioids and possibly to increase absorption) carries no reference.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite it as the bodies' recommendation, not as a tested finding.
