design_detail: Short report (Health & Justice 9, article 34): single-group before-and-after evaluation, filed as a prospective cohort, of the SHIELD (Safety and Health Integration in the Enforcement of Laws on Drugs) training for law enforcement in Indiana. Three 3-hour sessions were held by Zoom in December 2020, March 2021 and June 2021, facilitated by the Indiana Law Enforcement Academy and led by a former police officer; they covered needle-stick injuries, officer mental health, the public safety benefits of harm reduction programmes and addiction treatment, and a 10-minute module on fentanyl exposure. Of 204 attendees from 49 Indiana counties, 129 completed a baseline survey immediately before the training and 69 completed a follow-up survey that could be linked to their baseline by a code derived from name and date of birth. One item, rated on a 6-point scale (1 = strongly agree to 6 = strongly disagree), asked whether first responders who encounter fentanyl “are at great risk of overdose by touching it or inhaling it”. Analyses: descriptive statistics, chi-square, ANOVA, and independent and paired t-tests (SPSS). Appraised with ROBINS-I, as for sc_winograd_2020 and sc_park_2020. Tables 1 and 2 have no text layer and were read from the rendered pages.
can_establish: How many of 129 Indiana officers attending a SHIELD training agreed, before it, that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it, and how the 69 who completed the linked follow-up answered afterwards.
cannot_establish: Whether the training, let alone its 10-minute module, caused the change (no comparison group, and the follow-up came after the corrective message), whether the change lasted or altered behaviour, or how the 135 attendees without a follow-up survey would have answered; nor anything about the actual risk of touching or inhaling fentanyl.

sample.recruitment: Law enforcement officials attending SHIELD trainings facilitated by the Indiana Law Enforcement Academy, from 49 Indiana counties (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 2). Whether attendance was voluntary or assigned is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated beyond attendance. Roles at baseline included patrol, administration, community corrections, detective, community affairs or outreach, narcotics and other (Table 1, p. 3).
sample.demographics: Baseline, n = 129 (Table 1, p. 3): mean age 45.1 (SD 10.7); 97 male (75.2%), 32 female (24.8%); 109 White (84.5%), 10 Black (7.8%), 6 Hispanic (4.7%), 4 other (3.1%); education high school 16, some college 30, associate's degree 17, bachelor's degree 49 (38.0%), post-baccalaureate degree 17; 27 (20.9%) with 0–3 years in law enforcement and 29 (22.5%) with more than 25; patrol 40 (31.0%), administration 32 (24.8%), community corrections 16 (12.4%); prior fentanyl exposure training 79 (61.2%). Follow-up completers, n = 69: mean age 45.1 (SD 10.7); 51 male (73.9%); 58 White (84.1%); 32 with a bachelor's degree (46.4%) and 5 with high school only (7.2%); 23 patrol (33.3%); 46 with prior fentanyl exposure training (66.7%).
sample.attrition: 129 of 204 attendees (63.2%) completed the baseline survey and 69 of the 129 (53.5%) the follow-up, 34% of attendees overall (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 2; Abstract, p. 1). The authors report no significant demographic differences between completers and baseline-only respondents (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 4); baseline belief is not compared, although the completers' baseline mean (2.2) was close to that of all 129 (2.3).
sample.selection_effects: Attendees of one state's training programme during the COVID-19 pandemic, with about a third of attendees in the pre–post comparison. Completers more often held a bachelor's degree (46.4% vs 38.0%) and less often had high school only (7.2% vs 12.4%) than all baseline respondents (Table 1). Over half had prior fentanyl exposure precaution training, which the authors characterize as the misinformation the module corrects (p. 3); its content was not assessed.

exposure.measurement: Attendance at one 3-hour SHIELD session by Zoom (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 2). The fentanyl module emphasized that a nicotine transdermal patch is specially formulated to promote absorption through the skin, an effect that exposing skin to tobacco cannot achieve, and that the same principle applies to fentanyl; that people routinely process and package illicit fentanyl in large quantities in confined spaces without reported transdermal or inhalation overdoses or evidence of precautions; and that false beliefs about fentanyl's lethality can produce physical reactions consistent with severe panic, which are inconsistent with exposure to fentanyl (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to drug doses: one 3-hour session with a 10-minute fentanyl module.

comparison.controls: None: single-group pre–post among the 69 linked respondents; baseline comparisons by respondent characteristics among the 129.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Without a comparison group, the change cannot be separated from answering the item a second time, from demand characteristics after a corrective message, or from the remaining 170 minutes of training. The content of officers' prior fentanyl training and their media exposure were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: One item on a 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly agree, 2 = agree, 3 = somewhat agree, 4 = somewhat disagree, 5 = disagree, 6 = strongly disagree) on whether first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching it or inhaling it (Methods, 3rd paragraph, p. 2; Table 2 note, p. 4). The baseline survey was given during time allotted at the start of the training; the follow-up was online.
outcomes.validity_norms: Single unvalidated item that combines two routes (touching or inhaling) and a degree (great risk), so disagreement may concern the degree of risk rather than any risk.
outcomes.operationalization: Agreement: strongly agree, agree or somewhat agree; disagreement: the three disagree options. Change: the paired difference in mean score among the 69.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: baseline comparisons by education, role, age, race, gender, length of service and prior training, the same comparisons at follow-up, and the paired test, all at p < .05.

analysis.effect_sizes: Baseline, n = 129 (Table 2, p. 4): 52 strongly agree, 42 agree, 9 somewhat agree, 6 somewhat disagree, 8 disagree, 12 strongly disagree; 103 agreed (79.8%) and 26 disagreed (20.2%); mean 2.3 (SD 1.6). Follow-up, n = 69: 9, 8, 10, 8, 12 and 22 respectively; 27 agreed (39.1%) and 42 disagreed (60.9%); mean 4.0 (SD 1.8). Paired t-test among the 69: mean 2.2 to 4.0, t = 6.52, p < .001, with a printed 95% CI [1.05, 0.51] and Cohen's d = 2.33. At baseline, respondents with a college degree (n = 83) scored 2.5 against 1.9 for those without (t = 2.17, printed 95% CI [1.14, 0.05], printed Cohen's d = 2.33, p = .032); role differed (F = 2.71, p = .017), patrol against others 2.6 against 1.8 (t = 2.95, 95% CI [0.26, 1.32], printed Cohen's d = 1.61, p = .004); no differences by age, race, gender, length of service or prior fentanyl-related training (Results, 2nd–3rd paragraphs, p. 4). Editors' calculations: Wilson 95% CIs 72.1 to 85.9% for baseline agreement and 28.5 to 50.9% for follow-up agreement; standardized effects recomputed from t and n are about d = 0.40 (degree, 83 vs 46), d = 0.56 (patrol, 40 vs 89) and d_z = 0.78 (paired, n = 69); the 95% CI for the paired mean change of 1.8 points is about 1.25 to 2.35. The printed paired interval [0.51, 1.05] matches the interval for d_z (about 0.52 to 1.05), and the printed 2.33 matches the SD of the paired differences (about 2.3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the study is presented as confirming the findings of an earlier pilot (Winograd et al., 2020) (Discussion, p. 4). Approved as exempt by the Wayne State University IRB as a minimal-risk training evaluation (#2020037) (pp. 2, 5).
analysis.selective_reporting: The completers' baseline answers are given only as a mean (2.2), not as percentages, so the abstract's comparison of 79.8% (of 129) with 39.1% (of 69) mixes denominators.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; the authors say 69 respondents is a small number that limits confidence in the conclusions (p. 4).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Before a 3-hour SHIELD training, 103 of 129 Indiana officers (79.8%) agreed that first responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it, 52 of them strongly. Of the 69 who completed the linked follow-up, 27 (39.1%) still agreed and 22 strongly disagreed; their mean score moved from 2.2 to 4.0 on the 6-point scale (t = 6.52; d_z about 0.8 by editors' calculation). Two-thirds of attendees are missing from the pre–post comparison, and there was no comparison group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes a “10-min online training” (p. 1), whereas the Methods describe a 10-minute module within a 3-hour training that also covered needle-stick injuries, officer mental health, harm reduction and treatment (p. 2). The abstract sets 79.8% at baseline (of 129) against 39.1% at follow-up (of 69) with p < .001, a p-value that comes from the paired t-test on the means of 69. The Discussion says the analysis “confirms that a brief training module” had a corrective effect and that the intervention had a “considerable effect” (p. 4), relying on printed effect sizes that do not match the data (see reporting issues), and suggests that a training video with similar content shown at roll calls holds promise, although no video was tested. The authors acknowledge the low follow-up response, that knowledge rather than behaviour was measured and that persistence was not examined (pp. 4–5), but argue that the attrition does not necessarily indicate non-response bias, on the basis of demographic comparisons only.

timeline.event: ACMT and AACT joint report, cited in its Clinical Toxicology printing (Moss et al., 2018) for very low risk from incidental transdermal exposure and for 200 minutes of breathing fentanyl at the highest airborne concentrations being needed to reach a therapeutic dose (p. 2); the record moss_2017 has the same title.
Persaud and Jennings (2020): survey of New York first responders, cited as finding that 80% believed briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly (p. 2); not read.

Winograd et al. (2020), the pilot this study sets out to confirm, with two of the same authors: after a training with a 10-minute segment, the share of 140 Missouri responders answering False to a statement that they could overdose from touching fentanyl rose from 20.9% to 83.6% (card sc_winograd_2020). This paper describes those figures as concerning 113 officers (p. 2).

Beletsky et al. (2020), with two of the same authors, cited for social media posts reaching 70 million viewers or more (p. 2), a figure that study presents as an upper bound on potential views (card sc_beletsky_2020).
Herman et al. (2020), cited for no reported exposure incident having been confirmed as an overdose (p. 2); not read for this card.
Attaway et al. (2021), cited for misinformation spreading through policing networks and the need for corrective messaging (pp. 1–2) (card sc_attaway_2021).
This study published (received 10 September, published online 24 November 2021).

replication.where_it_stands: Two uncontrolled before-and-after studies by overlapping teams (Winograd et al., 2020; this study) found that first responders' agreement with the belief fell after a training that included a short fentanyl module, measured at or soon after the training with different single items. No controlled evaluation, delayed follow-up or behavioural outcome appears in the sources read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I asks whether the study can estimate the effect of the training on officers' belief. It cannot: there is no comparison group, two-thirds of attendees are missing from the pre–post comparison, the outcome is one double-barrelled item answered after the corrective message, and the printed effect sizes are wrong. Citable for: the share of these Indiana officers agreeing with the statement before training (103 of 129, 79.8%) and the answers of the 69 who completed the follow-up (27 still agreeing, 39.1%). Not citable for: the size or persistence of a training effect, the effect of the 10-minute module alone, or behaviour.

design_detail: Brief report (Harm Reduct J 17, article 58): single-group before-and-after evaluation, filed as a prospective cohort, of an overdose education and response training for emergency responders in the Eastern Region of Missouri. Between January and August 2019 project staff ran eight law enforcement and three EMS trainings reaching 200 participants; 140 were analysed (113 law enforcement or security officers, the LEO group; 27 EMS, EMT or fire department workers, the EMS group). The training, about 2 hours long, covered addiction, harm reduction, naloxone-related risk compensation, treatment medications and Missouri's naloxone and Good Samaritan laws, and included about 10 minutes on the medical impossibility of overdose from incidental skin contact with fentanyl, taught by an emergency medicine physician in LEO trainings and by the project manager in EMS trainings. A paper survey was completed just before and immediately after the training; only one True/False item was analysed. Differences between professions were tested with Fisher's exact test and pre–post change with McNemar's test. Appraised with ROBINS-I because the training is an intervention and the paper infers its effect, as for sc_park_2020.
can_establish: How these 140 Missouri emergency responders answered True or False to “I can overdose from touching fentanyl.” just before and immediately after a training that included a 10-minute corrective segment, overall and by profession.
cannot_establish: Whether the training caused a lasting change of belief (no comparison group, and the same item was answered again immediately after the trainer had given the answer), whether the 10-minute segment alone produced it (it was part of a 2-hour training), whether responders acted differently at overdose scenes, or anything about the actual risk of touching fentanyl.

sample.recruitment: Attendees of 11 trainings (8 for law enforcement, 3 for EMS) run by project staff in the Eastern Region of Missouri, January to August 2019, as part of a broader effort to improve community access to naloxone (Introduction, last paragraph, and Methods › Participants, p. 2). How agencies and attendees came to the trainings is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Trainings were tailored for professional emergency responders; other professionals could attend, but their surveys were omitted (n = 17) (Methods › Participants, p. 2). No other criteria are stated, and whether the analysis required both surveys is not stated.
sample.demographics: Table 1 (p. 3), N = 140: mean age 40.96 (SD 11.27); 110 men (printed 79.7%); 115 White (82.1%), 15 Black (10.7%), 4 multiracial or other (2.9%), 6 refused (4.3%); 5 Hispanic or Latino(a) (3.6%). LEO group (n = 113): mean age 40.6 (SD 11.0), 98 men (86.7%), 89 White (78.8%), 15 Black (13.3%). EMS group (n = 27): mean age 42.3 (SD 12.5), 12 men (44.4%), 26 White (96.3%).
sample.attrition: 200 participants were reached; 17 other professionals were omitted and 140 analysed, leaving 43 (21.5% of 200) unaccounted for (editors' subtraction; the paper does not explain them). The number with both a pre and a post survey is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: One region of one state; responders were predominantly White and male, which the authors name as a limit to generalizability (p. 4); the LEO group includes security officers; the EMS group is small (27). The 43 unexplained participants may include people who missed one of the two surveys.

exposure.measurement: Everyone analysed attended the training (Methods › Procedure, 1st paragraph, p. 2). Its content: addiction as a chronic brain disease, harm reduction principles, concerns about enabling drug use (naloxone-related risk compensation), addiction treatment medications, Missouri's naloxone and Good Samaritan laws, and accurate information on the medical impossibility of overdosing from incidental skin exposure to fentanyl, which took about 10 minutes to present and discuss. The fentanyl segment was taught by an emergency medicine physician in LEO trainings and by the project manager in EMS trainings. The whole training lasted about 2 hours (Limitations and future directions, p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to drug doses: one session of about 2 hours, with about 10 minutes on fentanyl contact.

comparison.controls: None: single-group pre–post. The LEO and EMS groups were compared with each other at each time point (Fisher's exact test).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: With no comparison group and an immediate post-test, the change cannot be separated from answering the same item twice, from wanting to give the answer just taught (demand characteristics) or from the other modules of the training; the two professions also had different presenters (physician or project manager). Prior fentanyl training and media exposure were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: One original item, answered True or False before and after the training: “I can overdose from touching fentanyl.” (Methods › Measure of belief in fentanyl exposure risk, p. 2). The paper survey also had items on overdose recognition and response, which were not analysed in this paper (Procedure, 2nd paragraph, p. 2). Surveys were later entered into REDCap by a research assistant.
outcomes.validity_norms: Single unvalidated item; no reliability or validity data.
outcomes.operationalization: Correct answer: False. Outcome: the proportion answering False before and after the training.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; five tests on the one item (two Fisher's exact tests, three McNemar's tests). Other survey items were not reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-completed paper survey). How the pre and post surveys were linked for the paired analysis, and whether they were anonymous, is not described.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages and p-values only (Results, pp. 2–3; Fig. 1, p. 3). Before training, 20.9% of all participants answered False; LEO 16.8%, EMS 37.0% (Fisher's exact p = .033). After training, 83.6% answered False (a 62.7-point difference; McNemar's p < .001); LEO 81.4% and EMS 92.6% (each McNemar's p < .001), increases of 64.6 and 55.6 points; the professions did not differ significantly after training (Fisher's p = .301). Editors' calculations from the group percentages and sizes: LEO 19/113 before and 92/113 after, EMS 10/27 and 25/27, all 29/140 (20.7%) and 117/140 (83.6%). Wilson 95% CIs: all participants 14.8 to 28.2% before and 76.6 to 88.8% after; LEO after 73.3 to 87.5%; EMS after 76.6 to 97.9%. Discordant pairs are not reported; at least 88 people must have changed from True to False. Two-sided Fisher's exact p recomputed from these counts: 0.032 before (matches the printed .033) and 0.25 after (printed .301).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned. Approved by the University of Missouri–St. Louis IRB (registration number 00000756); consent forms were signed before the pre-training survey (Ethics approval and consent to participate, p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the fentanyl item of a multi-item survey is analysed, which the authors state (p. 2). The number answering each survey, the paired n and the discordant counts are not given.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; the authors note the relatively small sample (p. 4).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Just before training, about four in five of these Missouri responders did not answer False to the statement that they could overdose from touching fentanyl (20.9% answered False; 16.8% of the LEO group and 37.0% of the EMS group). Immediately after a 2-hour training with a 10-minute corrective segment, 83.6% answered False (LEO 81.4%, EMS 92.6%). There was no comparison group and no later follow-up, and 140 of 200 participants were analysed.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says the authors determined that the 10-minute presentation “reduces emergency responders' endorsement of the belief they could overdose” (p. 3); the Conclusions call the study the “first to demonstrate the effectiveness of a training intervention” (p. 4); the title speaks of early evidence of success. The Limitations, however, say the simple design prevented assessing confounding or drawing causal inferences, and that the 2-hour training included other modules, so whether a brief fentanyl-focused training suffices remains to be studied (p. 4). The non-significant post-training difference between professions (p = .301, with 27 in the EMS group) is read as the difference going away, and the pre-training difference is attributed, without data, to EMS personnel's medical training and less contact with police and DEA colleagues (p. 3). Answers given immediately after the trainer stated the correct answer show what participants reported then, not a lasting change of belief or behaviour; the authors acknowledge that behaviour was not linked (p. 4). The Introduction's statement that overdose from incidental skin contact is a medical impossibility cites two press articles, one of them a newspaper opinion piece, followed by the ACMT/AACT statement and a NIOSH database entry for the claim having been debunked (p. 1; references 14–16 and 26, p. 5); the study measures belief, not risk.

timeline.event: ACMT and AACT position statement, cited in its Clinical Toxicology printing (Moss et al., 2018) as officially debunking overdose from incidental contact (p. 1); the record moss_2017 has the same title.

Persaud and Jennings (2019): survey of 247 New York first responders, cited as finding that 80% believed briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, and as the only earlier study of responders' perceptions (p. 2); not read.
Herman et al. (2020), cited for over 150 media reports of first responder exposures to opioids in 2017 (p. 1); not read for this card.
This study published (received 27 May, published online 24 August 2020).
Attaway et al. (2021) cite this study for a brief presentation reducing responders' belief that they could overdose from contact (p. 5) (card sc_attaway_2021).

del Pozo et al. (2021), with two of the same authors (Goulka, Beletsky), set out to confirm this study among Indiana officers: agreement with a different 6-point item fell from 79.8% of 129 at baseline to 39.1% of 69 at follow-up. They describe this study's 20.9% to 83.6% as concerning 113 officers, although those figures are for all 140 responders (card sc_del_pozo_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: One further uncontrolled before-and-after study, by an overlapping team with a different item, found change in the same direction, smaller and with heavy attrition (del Pozo et al., 2021). No controlled or randomized evaluation, delayed follow-up or behavioural outcome appears in the sources read; the authors call for testing a stand-alone fentanyl-focused training and for linking beliefs to behaviour (p. 4).

funding.affiliations_note: Missouri Institute of Mental Health, University of Missouri–St. Louis (four authors); National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Abuse, St. Louis; Northeastern University (Goulka, Beletsky), whose authors also wrote Beletsky et al. what_would_settle_it: A cluster-randomized trial in which training sessions or agencies receive the standard overdose training with or without the fentanyl segment (or the segment against an attention control), measured with a validated multi-item scale that separates touching from inhaling, at a delayed follow-up of weeks to months with complete paired data, and with recorded behaviour at overdose scenes (time to naloxone, protective equipment, calls for hazmat teams).

domains.domain: Bias due to confounding
domains.note: No comparison group: the immediate pre–post change cannot be separated from answering the item a second time, from demand characteristics just after the trainer gave the answer, or from the rest of the 2-hour training. The comparison between professions is also confounded by presenter.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Attendees of trainings in one region, selection of agencies and attendees not described; 140 of 200 participants analysed, 43 of them unexplained.

domains.domain: Bias in classification of interventions
domains.note: Everyone analysed attended the training. The intervention received is the whole 2-hour training, not the 10-minute segment that the Discussion names.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Content was tailored to the audience and the fentanyl segment was delivered by different presenters for the two professions; fidelity was not recorded.

domains.domain: Bias due to missing data
domains.note: 43 participants (21.5%) are unaccounted for; the paired n is not reported, and the overall pre-training percentage implies a different denominator from the group figures.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of outcomes
domains.note: One unvalidated True/False item, self-completed in the training room immediately after the correct answer had been taught; respondents knew what the training wanted them to answer.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Only one item of a multi-item survey is reported, although it is the stated aim; paired counts are not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I asks whether the study can estimate the effect of the training on belief. It cannot: there is no comparison group, the post-test came immediately after the answer was taught, the outcome is one self-completed item, and 43 participants are unexplained. Citable for: how common the belief was among these Missouri responders before training (20.9% answered False to “I can overdose from touching fentanyl.”; LEO 16.8%, EMS 37.0%) and what they answered immediately afterwards (83.6% False). Not citable for: a lasting or causal change in belief, the effect of the 10-minute segment alone, or any change in behaviour.

key_findings.finding: Eleven trainings (8 for law enforcement, 3 for EMS) held January to August 2019 in the Eastern Region of Missouri reached 200 participants; surveys of 17 other professionals were omitted, and 140 were analysed: 113 in the LEO group (law enforcement or security officers) and 27 in the EMS group (EMS, EMT or fire department workers).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants

key_findings.finding: The training covered addiction, harm reduction principles, naloxone-related risk compensation, treatment medications and Missouri's naloxone and Good Samaritan laws; the segment on the medical impossibility of overdosing from incidental skin exposure to fentanyl took about 10 minutes and was taught by an emergency medicine physician (LEO trainings) or the project manager (EMS trainings); the whole training lasted about 2 hours.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedure, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Limitations and future directions (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Participants completed a paper survey after giving consent and again immediately after the training; the item analysed asked them to check True or False for “I can overdose from touching fentanyl.”, and only this item was analysed.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedure, 2nd paragraph; Measure of belief in fentanyl exposure risk

key_findings.finding: Before training, 20.9% of all participants answered False; 16.8% of the LEO group and 37.0% of the EMS group (Fisher's exact test, p = .033).
key_findings.locator: Results › Baseline differences by profession (starts p. 2, continues p. 3)
key_findings.note: The group figures correspond to 19/113 and 10/27, which give 29/140 = 20.7% overall rather than 20.9% (editors' calculation); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Immediately after training, 83.6% of all participants answered False (a 62.7-point difference from before; McNemar's test, p < .001); 81.4% of the LEO group and 92.6% of the EMS group (each McNemar's p < .001), increases of 64.6 and 55.6 points; the post-training proportions did not differ significantly between professions (Fisher's exact test, p = .301).

key_findings.note: The paper calls the differences percentages; they are percentage points. The post-training Fisher p recomputed from 92/113 and 25/27 is 0.25 (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Participants (N = 140) had a mean age of 40.96 (SD 11.27); 110 were men (printed 79.7%), 115 White (82.1%) and 15 Black (10.7%). The LEO group was 86.7% men (98 of 113) and the EMS group 44.4% (12 of 27).
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations the predominantly White, male Midwestern sample, the small sample and simple design that prevented advanced analyses, assessment of confounding and causal inference, the lack of information linking beliefs to behaviour or agency protocols, and the 2-hour training's other modules, which leave open whether a brief fentanyl-focused training is sufficient.
key_findings.locator: Limitations and future directions

key_findings.finding: The Discussion states that the authors determined that a brief, 10-minute presentation and discussion reduces responders' endorsement of the belief and that endorsement varied between the LEO and EMS groups, adding that their results suggest LEOs are more likely than EMS personnel to hold it and that the difference goes away after the presentation; the Conclusions call the study, to the authors' knowledge, the first to demonstrate the effectiveness of a training intervention in correcting the misconception.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Conclusions (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The authors' interpretation; see the interpretation gap and the Limitations on the same pages.

reporting_issues.issue: Of 200 participants, 17 other professionals were omitted and 140 analysed; the rest (by the editors' subtraction, 43) are not accounted for.
reporting_issues.consequence: If they are people who missed a survey, the analysis is of completers only and the direction of any bias is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The overall pre-training figure of 20.9% does not match the group figures of 16.8% of 113 and 37.0% of 27; by the editors' calculation these are 19 and 10 people, 29/140 = 20.7%, and 20.9% would fit 29/139.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; it suggests a missing answer or a typing error. With 20.7% the overall change would be 62.9 points.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints 110 men as 79.7% of the overall sample of 140, while the group percentages use the full 113 and 27; by the editors' calculation 110/140 = 78.6%, and 79.7% fits a denominator of 138.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; denominators are inconsistent within the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The post-training comparison of professions is printed as Fisher's exact p = .301, from 81.4% of 113 and 92.6% of 27 answering False; in the editors' recomputation from those proportions (92/113 vs 25/27) the two-sided p is 0.25, while the pre-training p (.033) reproduces as 0.032.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the conclusion (no significant difference) is unchanged, but the printed value may come from different counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods use McNemar's test for paired data but do not say how pre and post surveys were linked or how many pairs there were, and give no discordant counts; the ethics statement refers to each pre and/or post-training test, implying that some participants completed only one.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paired analysis cannot be checked, and whether all 140 had both surveys is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that the 10-minute presentation reduces responders' endorsement of the belief, and the Conclusions that the study is the first to demonstrate the effectiveness of a training intervention, while the Limitations (p. 4) say the simple design prevented drawing causal inferences and that the 2-hour training contained other modules.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the change as answers before and immediately after a 2-hour training, not as an effect of the 10-minute segment.
